title: Acute Joint Pain Differential Diagnosis
description: Differential diagnosis for acute joint pain in adults, covering monoarthritis and polyarthritis etiologies including crystal-induced, infectious, inflammatory, and degenerative causes.
source_description: Ma L, Cranney A, Holroyd-Leduc JM. Acute monoarthritis: What is the cause of my patient's painful swollen joint? CMAJ 2009;180(1):59-65.

diagnoses.name: Septic Arthritis
key_features: Joint pain (85% of patients) with swelling (78%)
Acute onset over hours to days
Warm, erythematous joint with restricted range of motion
Fever may be absent in immunocompromised patients
red_flags: Recent joint surgery or prosthetic joint
Risk factors: age >80, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, immunosuppression
recommended_tests: Synovial fluid aspiration with Gram stain and culture
Synovial fluid leukocyte count (>50,000/uL suggests infection)

diagnoses.name: Disseminated Gonococcal Infection
key_features: Most common nontraumatic acute monoarthritis in young sexually active adults
Migratory polyarthralgia preceding monoarthritis
Dermatitis-arthritis syndrome with vesiculopustular skin lesions
Tenosynovitis especially of wrists and hands
red_flags: Sexually active young adult with acute joint pain
Skin lesions with migratory joint pain
Positive urogenital or pharyngeal gonococcal testing
recommended_tests: Urogenital and pharyngeal NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Synovial fluid leukocyte count and differential

diagnoses.name: Gout (Crystal Arthropathy)
key_features: Rapid onset of severe joint pain, often nocturnal
First MTP joint involvement (podagra) classic but not universal
15-27% of acute monoarthritis cases
History of hyperuricemia, diuretic use, alcohol consumption
red_flags: Concurrent septic arthritis (gout and infection may coexist)
recommended_tests: Synovial fluid polarized microscopy (negatively birefringent MSU crystals)

diagnoses.name: Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition (Pseudogout)
key_features: Acute onset mimicking gout
Knee and wrist most commonly affected
Associated with hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesemia
Chondrocalcinosis on radiography
red_flags: Young patient with CPPD suggesting metabolic disease
recommended_tests: Synovial fluid polarized microscopy (weakly positive birefringent CPPD crystals)
Calcium, phosphate, magnesium, ferritin, TSH if metabolic cause suspected

diagnoses.name: Osteoarthritis (Acute Flare)
key_features: 5-17% of acute monoarthritis cases
Pain worsened by activity, relieved by rest
Morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes
Crepitus, bony enlargement, and tenderness on examination
red_flags: Effusion with inflammatory synovial fluid (consider alternative diagnosis)
recommended_tests: Synovial fluid analysis (noninflammatory: clear, viscous, WBC <2000/uL)
ESR and CRP to exclude inflammatory cause

diagnoses.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
key_features: 11-16% of acute monoarthritis presentations
Symmetric polyarthritis of MCP and PIP joints
Morning stiffness lasting more than 60 minutes
May initially present as monoarthritis before progressing
red_flags: Extra-articular manifestations (rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease)
recommended_tests: Joint radiography of hands and feet

diagnoses.name: Reactive Arthritis
key_features: Asymmetric oligoarthritis following genitourinary or GI infection
Onset typically within one month of preceding infection
Lower extremity predominance
Associated conjunctivitis, urethritis, mucocutaneous lesions

diagnoses.name: Psoriatic Arthritis
key_features: Develops in approximately 24% of psoriasis patients
Asymmetric oligoarthritis or polyarthritis
Dactylitis (sausage digits) and enthesitis
DIP joint involvement distinguishes from RA
recommended_tests: Skin and nail examination for psoriasis

diagnoses.name: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
key_features: Non-erosive symmetric polyarthritis
Arthritis of PIP joints and knees common
Associated malar rash, photosensitivity, serositis
Multisystem involvement

diagnoses.name: Traumatic Arthritis / Hemarthrosis
key_features: History of recent trauma or injury
Joint effusion with or without bloody aspirate
Mechanical symptoms (locking, instability) suggest internal derangement
Periarticular tenderness and ecchymosis
red_flags: Hemarthrosis without trauma (consider coagulopathy or tumor)
Fat droplets in aspirate suggesting intra-articular fracture
recommended_tests: Coagulation studies if no trauma history

diagnoses.name: Lyme Arthritis
key_features: Late manifestation of Borrelia burgdorferi infection
Intermittent monoarthritis, especially of the knee
History of tick exposure or erythema migrans rash
Endemic geographic area exposure
recommended_tests: Two-tier Lyme serology (ELISA followed by Western blot)
Synovial fluid PCR for Borrelia if serology equivocal

also_consider.name: Polymyalgia Rheumatica
also_consider.rationale: Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain with marked morning stiffness in adults over 50; dramatically responsive to low-dose corticosteroids

also_consider.name: Viral Arthritis (Parvovirus B19, Hepatitis B/C, HIV)
also_consider.rationale: Symmetric polyarthritis with viral prodrome; parvovirus causes RA-like presentation, hepatitis B causes PAN-associated arthritis

also_consider.name: Avascular Necrosis (Osteonecrosis)
also_consider.rationale: Insidious hip or knee pain worsened by weight-bearing; risk factors include corticosteroid use, alcohol, sickle cell disease

also_consider.name: Sarcoid Arthropathy
also_consider.rationale: Acute polyarthritis with erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (Lofgren syndrome); or chronic granulomatous arthritis

also_consider.name: Hemochromatosis-Associated Arthropathy
also_consider.rationale: Second and third MCP joint involvement with hook-like osteophytes; associated with CPPD; check ferritin and transferrin saturation

also_consider.name: Inflammatory Bowel Disease-Associated Arthritis
also_consider.rationale: Peripheral oligoarthritis correlating with bowel disease activity; axial disease independent of GI flares

also_consider.name: Behcet Disease
also_consider.rationale: Recurrent monoarthritis or oligoarthritis with oral/genital ulcers and uveitis; more common in Mediterranean and East Asian populations

also_consider.name: Familial Mediterranean Fever
also_consider.rationale: Recurrent monoarthritis episodes lasting 24-72 hours with serositis; Mediterranean descent; colchicine-responsive

also_consider.name: Pigmented Villonodular Synovitis
also_consider.rationale: Chronic monoarticular swelling with hemorrhagic effusion; MRI shows characteristic hemosiderin deposits

also_consider.name: Synovial Chondromatosis
also_consider.rationale: Monoarticular pain with locking and catching; radiography shows calcified loose bodies within the joint

also_consider.name: Tumor (Synovial Sarcoma or Metastatic Disease)
also_consider.rationale: Persistent monoarticular pain unresponsive to treatment; consider imaging if pain is disproportionate to exam findings

also_consider.name: Whipple Disease
also_consider.rationale: Migratory polyarthritis preceding GI symptoms by years; diagnosis by duodenal biopsy showing PAS-positive macrophages

clinical_reasoning_prompt: This is an evidence-based reference set, not an exhaustive differential. The most critical diagnostic step in acute monoarthritis is arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis -- crystal examination and culture are essential to distinguish crystal arthropathy from septic arthritis. Gout and septic arthritis may coexist. In polyarticular presentations, consider the pattern (symmetric vs asymmetric, small vs large joints) and duration (<6 weeks acute, >6 weeks chronic) to narrow the differential. Always assess for extra-articular features that may point to a systemic disease.
